messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Aisha Rahman was 66 and had spent most of her adult life as a midwife in a busy American city hospital, a role that had once given her a sense of purpose and calm competence. Her husband had long since grown used to her long shifts and her habit of moving briskly from one task to the next, and until recently she had assumed that this lifelong steadiness was simply who she was. That changed after a military deployment many years earlier, when she was working in a conflict zone as part of a medical relief team. One evening she was called to a compound near the base to assist with an emergency birth, and the scene unravelled into chaos: men in uniform entering and exiting in a rush, shouted commands, boots on hard ground, and one soldier repeatedly standing in the doorway while she tried to work. Aisha could still remember the unbearable feeling of being watched as she bent over the patient, the sense that the soldier’s gaze pinned her in place and that any mistake would bring consequences she could not manage. What frightened her most now was that the memory did not stay in the past; it lived on in her body whenever she found herself alone with a man, when a uniform came into view, or when someone seemed to be looking at her too closely.

After that experience, Aisha became constantly watchful. She found herself scanning faces, doorways, and exits without meaning to, and she was irritated by how quickly her body reacted to sudden movements from other people, as though she needed only a flash of motion to become immediately on guard. Even in places she knew were safe, she could not truly relax. At home she sat facing the room, not the wall, and in public she noticed her shoulders tightening whenever a man stood near her or someone in uniform crossed her path. At work, the hospital corridors were filled with triggers she could not avoid entirely: a security guard in a dark jacket, a maintenance worker stepping into a doorway, a physician’s abrupt turn toward her at the nurses’ station. Those moments stirred the same state of alertness she had known during the deployment, and she felt herself bracing before she had time to think. She had come to believe that danger could appear without warning, and that if she let her attention drift for even a moment, she might miss the one sign that would protect her.

To manage that sense of threat, Aisha threw herself into work and tasks with unusual intensity. She volunteered for extra shifts, stayed late to finish charts, reorganised supply cupboards, and moved from one chore to another until there was no quiet moment left for her thoughts to catch up with her. She also made sure never to be alone with another person if she could help it, especially not with men; she arranged to have nurses or clerks nearby, asked for doors to remain open, and chose crowded hallways over empty ones. In the hospital and at home she was vigilant for dangerous people, watching how a person walked, how quickly they turned, whether they wore a uniform, whether they were too close. These habits gave her a short-lived sense of control, but they also kept the world looking full of possible threats. Because she was always watching, she noticed more things that frightened her: a man waiting outside an exam room, a uniformed officer at the entrance, a stranger pausing behind her with no explanation. The more she organised her life around not being cornered or surprised, the more often she found herself encountering exactly the cues that set her on edge, and each new scare confirmed her sense that vigilance was necessary.

Over time the pattern narrowed her life. She declined invitations if there might be men she did not know, stayed close to colleagues during breaks, and kept herself busy even at home so she would not have to sit with her thoughts. Her husband noticed that she rarely rested and that she seemed unable to settle, even after long days. Aisha herself described feeling as though she was “always on duty,” never fully back in the present. By the time she sought help, she was exhausted by the effort of staying safe and frightened that her watchfulness was no longer optional but the only thing standing between her and another overwhelming moment. She came to treatment hoping to regain some ability to relax in her own home and at work, and fearing that if she stopped scanning the world so carefully, she would miss the next sign of danger.
